claim: Precise temporal coordination between slow oscillations (SOs) and sleep spindles indexes declarative memory network development.
source: Previously, we demonstrated that precise temporal coordination between slow oscillations (SOs) and sleep spindles indexes declarative memory network development (Hahn et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Hahn et al., 2020)

claim: Juggling performance was impacted by sleep and time of day effects.
source: Juggling performance was impacted by sleep and time of day effects.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the juggling task across different retention intervals

claim: Improved task proficiency after sleep leads to an attenuation of the learning curve.
source: Critically, we found that improved task proficiency after sleep lead to an attenuation of the learning curve, suggesting a dynamic juggling learning process.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing inverse relationship between task proficiency and learning curve

claim: Adults have a more precise SO–spindle coupling than adolescents.
source: Advancing our previous findings, we identified a more precise SO–spindle coupling in adults compared to adolescents.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from individualized cross-frequency coupling analyses

claim: SO–spindle coupling precision over motor areas predicted overnight changes in task proficiency.
source: Importantly, coupling precision over motor areas predicted overnight changes in task proficiency and learning curve, indicating that SO–spindle coupling relates to the dynamic motor learning process.
evidence: Supported by correlational analyses between coupling strength and behavioral measures

claim: SO–spindle coupling precision over motor areas predicted overnight changes in learning curve.
source: Importantly, coupling precision over motor areas predicted overnight changes in task proficiency and learning curve, indicating that SO–spindle coupling relates to the dynamic motor learning process.
evidence: Supported by correlational analyses between coupling strength and behavioral measures

claim: Regionally specific, precisely coupled sleep oscillations support gross-motor learning.
source: Our results provide first evidence that regionally specific, precisely coupled sleep oscillations support gross-motor learning.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing coupling strength over motor areas predicts learning outcomes

claim: Sleep actively supports learning.
source: Sleep actively supports learning (Diekelmann and Born, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature

claim: Memories acquired during wakefulness are reactivated in the hippocampus during sharp-wave ripple events in sleep.
source: Memories acquired during wakefulness are reactivated in the hippocampus during sharp-wave ripple events in sleep (Wilson and McNaughton, 1994; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research

claim: Sharp-wave ripple events are nested within thalamocortical sleep spindles that mediate synaptic plasticity.
source: These events are nested within thalamocortical sleep spindles that mediate synaptic plasticity (Niethard et al., 2018; Rosanova and Ulrich, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research

claim: Sleep spindles are facilitated by the depolarizing phase of cortical SOs thereby forming SO–spindle complexes.
source: Sleep spindles in turn are thought to be facilitated by the depolarizing phase of cortical SOs thereby forming SO–spindle complexes during which the subcortical–cortical network communication is optimal for information transfer (Chauvette et al., 2012; Clemens et al., 2011; Helfrich et al., 2019; Helfrich et al., 2018; Latchoumane et al., 2017; Mölle et al., 2011; Ngo et al., 2020; Niethard et al., 2018; Schreiner et al., 2021; Staresina et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous research

claim: Precisely timed SO–spindle interaction mediates successful memory consolidation across the lifespan.
source: Several lines of research recently demonstrated that precisely timed SO–spindle interaction mediates successful memory consolidation across the lifespan (Hahn et al., 2020; Helfrich et al., 2018; Mikutta et al., 2019; Mölle et al., 2011; Muehlroth et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: SO–spindle coupling is related to neural integrity of memory structures such as medial prefrontal cortex, thalamus, hippocampus, and entorhinal cortex.
source: Critically, SO–spindle coupling as well as spindles and SOs in isolation are related to neural integrity of memory structures such as medial prefrontal cortex, thalamus, hippocampus, and entorhinal cortex (Helfrich et al., 2021; Helfrich et al., 2018; Ladenbauer et al., 2017; Mander et al., 2017; Muehlroth et al., 2019; Spanò et al., 2020; Winer et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: SO–spindle coupling indexes general efficiency of memory pathways.
source: Thus, converging evidence suggests that SO–spindle coupling does not only actively transfer mnemonic information during sleep but also indexes general efficiency of memory pathways (Helfrich et al., 2021; Mander et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations and inference from previous findings

claim: SO–spindle coordination becomes more consistent from childhood to late adolescence.
source: In our recent longitudinal work, we found that SO–spindle coordination was not only becoming more consistent from childhood to late adolescence but also directly predicted enhancements in declarative memory formation across those formative years (Hahn et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous longitudinal work

claim: SO–spindle coordination directly predicted enhancements in declarative memory formation from childhood to late adolescence.
source: In our recent longitudinal work, we found that SO–spindle coordination was not only becoming more consistent from childhood to late adolescence but also directly predicted enhancements in declarative memory formation across those formative years (Hahn et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous longitudinal work

claim: The active system consolidation theory assumes a crucial role of hippocampal memory replay for sleep-dependent memory consolidation.
source: However, because the active system consolidation theory assumes a crucial role of hippocampal memory replay for sleep-dependent memory consolidation, most studies, including our own, focused on the effect of SO–spindle coupling on hippocampus-dependent declarative memory consolidation.
evidence: Supported by established theoretical framework

claim: The role of SO–spindle coordination for motor learning or consolidation of procedural information remains poorly understood.
source: Therefore, the role of SO–spindle coordination for motor learning or consolidation of procedural information remains poorly understood.
evidence: Inference from the state of the literature

claim: Sleep's beneficial role for motor memory formation has been extensively investigated and frequently related to individual oscillatory activity of sleep spindles and SO.
source: While sleep's beneficial role for motor memory formation has been extensively investigated and frequently related to individual oscillatory activity of sleep spindles and SO (Barakat et al., 2011; Boutin et al., 2018; Fogel et al., 2017; Huber et al., 2004; King et al., 2017; Nishida and Walker, 2007; Pinsard et al., 2019; Tamaki et al., 2013; Tamaki et al., 2008; Vahdat et al., 2017; Walker et al., 2002), there is little empirical evidence for the involvement of the timed interplay between spindles and SO.
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: There is little empirical evidence for the involvement of the timed interplay between spindles and SO in motor memory formation.
source: While sleep's beneficial role for motor memory formation has been extensively investigated and frequently related to individual oscillatory activity of sleep spindles and SO (Barakat et al., 2011; Boutin et al., 2018; Fogel et al., 2017; Huber et al., 2004; King et al., 2017; Nishida and Walker, 2007; Pinsard et al., 2019; Tamaki et al., 2013; Tamaki et al., 2008; Vahdat et al., 2017; Walker et al., 2002), there is little empirical evidence for the involvement of the timed interplay between spindles and SO.
evidence: Inference from literature review

claim: In rodents, the neuronal firing pattern in the motor cortex was more coherent during spindles with close temporal proximity to SOs after engaging in a grasping motor task.
source: In rodents, the neuronal firing pattern in the motor cortex was more coherent during spindles with close temporal proximity to SOs after engaging in a grasping motor task (Silversmith et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to rodent study

claim: In humans, stronger SO–spindle coupling related to higher accuracy during mirror tracing.
source: In humans, stronger SO–spindle coupling related to higher accuracy during mirror tracing, a motor adaption task where subjects trace the line of a shape while looking through a mirror (Mikutta et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to human study

claim: Research has focused on laboratory suitable fine-motor sequence learning or motor adaption tasks, which has hampered understanding of memory consolidation for more ecologically valid gross-motor abilities.
source: So far, research focused on laboratory suitable fine-motor sequence learning or motor adaption tasks, which has hampered our understanding of memory consolidation for more ecologically valid gross-motor abilities that are crucial for our everyday life (for a review see King et al., 2017).
evidence: Inference from literature review with citation

claim: Overnight performance benefits for riding an inverse steering bike have been shown to be related to spindle activity in adolescents and adults.
source: Overnight performance benefits for riding an inverse steering bike have been shown to be related to spindle activity in adolescents and adults (Bothe et al., 2019; Bothe et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Juggling performance was supported by sleep.
source: Similarly, juggling performance was supported by sleep and juggling training induced power increments in the spindle and SO frequency range during a nap (Morita et al., 2012; Morita et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Juggling training induced power increments in the spindle and SO frequency range during a nap.
source: Similarly, juggling performance was supported by sleep and juggling training induced power increments in the spindle and SO frequency range during a nap (Morita et al., 2012; Morita et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Juggling has been found to induce lasting structural changes in the hippocampus and midtemporal areas outside of the motor network.
source: Remarkably, juggling has been found to induce lasting structural changes in the hippocampus and midtemporal areas outside of the motor network (Boyke et al., 2008; Draganski et al., 2004), making it a promising expedient to probe the active system consolidation framework for gross-motor memory.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Juggling is a promising expedient to probe the active system consolidation framework for gross-motor memory.
source: Remarkably, juggling has been found to induce lasting structural changes in the hippocampus and midtemporal areas outside of the motor network (Boyke et al., 2008; Draganski et al., 2004), making it a promising expedient to probe the active system consolidation framework for gross-motor memory.
evidence: Inference based on cited structural changes

claim: Complex gross-motor skill demands accurately executed movements that are coordinated by integrating visual, sensory, and motor information.
source: Importantly, this complex gross-motor skill demands accurately executed movements that are coordinated by integrating visual, sensory, and motor information.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about motor skill requirements

claim: SO and spindles become more tightly coupled across brain maturation which predicts declarative memory formation enhancements.
source: Previously, we demonstrated that SO and spindles become more tightly coupled across brain maturation which predicts declarative memory formation enhancements (Hahn et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work

claim: Adolescents improved their juggling performance over the course of all nine blocks.
source: Adolescents improved their juggling performance over the course of all nine blocks (Figure 2A, top; F3.957, 94.962 = 6.948, p < 0.001, η2 = 0.23).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and Figure 2A

claim: There was no overall difference in juggling performance between the sleep-first and wake-first groups in adolescents.
source: There was neither an overall difference in performance between the sleep-first and wake-first groups (F1, 24 = 1.002, p = 0.327, η2 = 0.04), nor did they differ over the course of the juggling blocks (F3.957, 94.962 = 1.148, p = 0.339, η2 = 0.05).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Adults improved in juggling performance across all 15 blocks.
source: Similar to the adolescents, adults improved in performance across all 15 blocks (Figure 2B, top; F4.673, 182.241 = 11.967, p < 0.001, η2 = 0.24), regardless of group (F4.673, 182.241 = 0.529, p = 0.742, η2 = 0.01).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and Figure 2B

claim: There was no overall difference in juggling performance between the sleep-first and wake-first groups in adults.
source: Further, there was no overall difference in performance between the sleep-first and wake-first groups in adults (F1, 39 = 1.398, p = 0.244, η2 = 0.04).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Participants do not reach asymptotic level juggling performance.
source: Collectively, these results show, that participants do not reach asymptotic level juggling performance (for single subject data of good and bad performers, see Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and supplementary figures

claim: The gross-motor skill learning process is still in progress in adolescents and adults.
source: In other words, the gross-motor skill learning process is still in progress in adolescents and adults.
evidence: Inference from the observation that participants do not reach asymptotic performance

claim: Participants in the sleep-first group showed a steeper learning curve than the wake-first group after the first retention interval.
source: A mixed ANOVA with the factors performance test (pre- and postretention interval), condition group (sleep-first and wake-first) and age group (adolescents and adults) showed a significant interaction between performance test and condition group (F1, 65 = 4.868, p = 0.031, η2 = 0.07). This result indicates that regardless of age, the juggling learning curve becomes steeper after sleep than after wakefulness, thus indicating that sleep impacts motor learning (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and Figure 2D

claim: Sleep impacts motor learning.
source: This result indicates that regardless of age, the juggling learning curve becomes steeper after sleep than after wakefulness, thus indicating that sleep impacts motor learning (Figure 2D).
evidence: Inference from statistical analysis showing interaction between performance test and condition group

claim: The adult sleep-first group had better overall task proficiency than the wake-first group.
source: When analyzing the task proficiency before and after the first retention interval, depending on condition and age group, we found a significant interaction between condition and age group (Figure 2E; F1, 65 = 5.210, p = 0.026, η2 = 0.07), showing that the adult sleep-first group had better overall task proficiency than the wake-first group, whereas the adolescent sleep-first group was worse than the wake-first group.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and Figure 2E

claim: The adolescent sleep-first group had worse overall task proficiency than the wake-first group.
source: When analyzing the task proficiency before and after the first retention interval, depending on condition and age group, we found a significant interaction between condition and age group (Figure 2E; F1, 65 = 5.210, p = 0.026, η2 = 0.07), showing that the adult sleep-first group had better overall task proficiency than the wake-first group, whereas the adolescent sleep-first group was worse than the wake-first group.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and Figure 2E

claim: Sleep influences learning of juggling as a gross-motor task.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that sleep influences learning of juggling as a gross-motor task.
evidence: Inference from multiple statistical analyses showing sleep effects

claim: Performance tests in the morning are characterized by a steeper learning curve than the evening tests.
source: Figure 2A, B indicates that performance tests in the morning might be characterized by a steeper learning curve than the evening tests. We confirmed this observation using a linear mixed model (Supplementary file 1—table 5A, B).
evidence: Supported by visual inspection of figures and statistical analysis

claim: Both time of day and sleep contribute to the overall juggling performance.
source: These results suggest that both time of day and sleep contribute to the overall juggling performance.
evidence: Inference from linear mixed model results

claim: A stronger increase in task proficiency across sleep leads to a flatter learning curve.
source: We hypothesized, that a stronger increase in task proficiency across sleep would lead to a flatter learning curve based on the assumption that motor skill learning involves fast and slow learning stages. Indeed, we confirmed a strong negative correlation between the change (postretention values − preretention values) in task proficiency and the change in learning curve after the retention interval (Figure 2F; rhos = −0.71, p < 0.001), which also remained strong after outlier removal (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by correlational analysis and Figure 2F

claim: Participants who consolidate their juggling performance after a retention interval show slower gains in performance.
source: This result indicates that participants who consolidate their juggling performance after a retention interval show slower gains in performance.
evidence: Inference from the negative correlation between task proficiency change and learning curve change

claim: The flattening of the learning curve does not necessarily indicate worse learning but rather marks a more progressed learning stage.
source: Note, that the flattening of the learning curve does not necessarily indicate worse learning but rather mark a more progressed learning stage.
evidence: Inference based on motor learning theory

claim: Spectral power was elevated in adolescents as compared to adults across the whole tested frequency range (0.1-20 Hz).
source: Spectral power was elevated in adolescents as compared to adults across the whole tested frequency range (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A left for representative electrode Cz; cluster test: p < 0.001, d = 1.88).
evidence: Supported by cluster-based permutation test and supplementary figure

claim: The power difference between adolescents and adults was explained by a spindle frequency peak shift and broadband decrease in the fractal or 1/f trend of the signal.
source: Similar to the previously reported developmental patterns of sleep oscillations from childhood to adolescence (Hahn et al., 2020), this difference was explained by a spindle frequency peak shift and broadband decrease in the fractal or 1/f trend of the signal, thus directly replicating and extending our previous findings in a separate sample.
evidence: Supported by data analysis and citation to previous work

claim: Adolescents exhibited a higher offset of fractal component on the y-axis than adults.
source: After estimating the fractal component of the power spectrum by means of irregular-resampling autospectral analysis (Wen and Liu, 2016), we found that adolescents exhibited a higher offset of fractal component on the y-axis than adults (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A middle; cluster test: p < 0.001, d = 1.99).
evidence: Supported by IRASA analysis and cluster test

claim: Adolescents and adults both display the expected topographical distribution of more pronounced frontal SO and centroparietal spindles.
source: Importantly, we observed the expected spatial amplitude topography with stronger frontal SO and pronounced centroparietal spindles for both age groups (Figure 3A left).
evidence: Supported by topographical analysis shown in Figure 3A

claim: Subjects displayed high interindividual variability in the sleep spindle range.
source: Importantly, subjects displayed high interindividual variability in the sleep spindle range and a gradual spindle frequency increase by age that is critically underestimated by the group average of the oscillatory residuals (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, right).
evidence: Supported by single subject data shown in Figure 3A right

claim: There is a gradual spindle frequency increase by age that is critically underestimated by the group average of the oscillatory residuals.
source: Importantly, subjects displayed high interindividual variability in the sleep spindle range and a gradual spindle frequency increase by age that is critically underestimated by the group average of the oscillatory residuals (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, right).
evidence: Supported by single subject data analysis

claim: Spindle frequency is faster at all but occipital electrodes in adults than in adolescents.
source: Even though we found the expected systematic spindle frequency increase in a frontoparietal cluster from adolescence to adulthood (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B; cluster test: p = 0.002, d = −0.87), both respective age groups showed a high degree of variability of the interindividual spindle peak.
evidence: Supported by cluster-based test shown in supplementary figure

claim: Both adolescent and adult age groups showed a high degree of variability of the interindividual spindle peak.
source: Even though we found the expected systematic spindle frequency increase in a frontoparietal cluster from adolescence to adulthood (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B; cluster test: p = 0.002, d = −0.87), both respective age groups showed a high degree of variability of the interindividual spindle peak.
evidence: Supported by analysis of individual spindle peaks

claim: There was no amplitude difference around the spindle peak between adolescents and adults after normalization.
source: Importantly, we found no amplitude differences around the spindle peak (point of SO-phase readout) between adolescents and adults using cluster-based random permutation testing (Figure 3B), indicating an unbiased analytical signal.
evidence: Supported by cluster-based permutation test on normalized data

claim: Adults had a higher coupling strength in a centroparietal cluster than adolescents.
source: As expected, adults had a higher coupling strength in a centroparietal cluster than adolescents (Figure 3C; cluster test: p < 0.001, d = 0.88), indicating a more precise interplay between SO and spindles during adulthood.
evidence: Supported by cluster-based test shown in Figure 3C

claim: Adults have a more precise interplay between SO and spindles than adolescents.
source: As expected, adults had a higher coupling strength in a centroparietal cluster than adolescents (Figure 3C; cluster test: p < 0.001, d = 0.88), indicating a more precise interplay between SO and spindles during adulthood.
evidence: Inference from coupling strength data

claim: Participants with a more consistent SO–spindle interplay have stronger overnight improvements in task proficiency.
source: We identified a significant central cluster (Figure 3D; mean rho = 0.37, p = 0.017), indicating that participants with a more consistent SO–spindle interplay have stronger overnight improvements in task proficiency.
evidence: Supported by cluster-corrected correlation analysis shown in Figure 3D

claim: Participants with a more precise SO–spindle coupling exhibit a flatter learning curve overnight.
source: Given this dependency, we observed a significant cluster-corrected correlation at C4 (Figure 3E; rhos = −0.45, p = 0.039, cluster-corrected), showing that participants with a more precise SO–spindle coupling exhibit a flatter learning curve overnight.
evidence: Supported by cluster-corrected correlation analysis shown in Figure 3E

claim: Individuals with high performance exhibit a smaller gain through additional training when approaching full task proficiency.
source: In other words, individuals with high performance exhibit a smaller gain through additional training when approaching full task proficiency.
evidence: Inference from the relationship between proficiency and learning curve

claim: Coupling strength predicts gross-motor learning dynamics in both adolescents and adults.
source: Critically, when computing the correlational analyses separately for adolescents and adults, we identified highly similar effects at electrode C4 for task proficiency (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C) and learning curve (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D) in each group. These complementary results demonstrate that coupling strength predicts gross-motor learning dynamics in both, adolescents and adults, and further shows that this effect is not solely driven by one group.
evidence: Supported by separate correlational analyses for each age group

claim: SO–spindle coupling strength remains remarkably stable between two nights.
source: First, we correlated SO–spindle coupling strength obtained from the adaptation night with the coupling strength in the learning night. We found that overall, coupling strength is highly correlated between the two measurements (mean rho across all channels = 0.55, Figure 3—figure supplement 2H), supporting the notion that coupling strength remains rather stable within the individual (i.e., trait).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis between two nights

claim: Coupling strength represents a trait effect rather than a state effect for motor learning.
source: Importantly, SO–spindle coupling still predicted learning dynamics on a single subject level advocating for a supportive function of sleep for gross-motor memory. Moreover, we found that SO–spindle coupling strength remains remarkably stable between two nights, which also explains why a learning-induced change in coupling strength did not relate to behavior (Figure 3—figure supplement 2I). Thus, our results primarily suggest that strength of SO–spindle coupling correlates with the ability to learn (trait), but does not solely convey the recently learned information.
evidence: Inference from stability analysis and lack of state effect

claim: Strong coupling indexes individuals with highly efficient subcortical–cortical network communication.
source: This set of findings is in line with recent ideas that strong coupling indexes individuals with highly efficient subcortical–cortical network communication (Helfrich et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to recent theoretical work

claim: SO–spindle coupling strength is likely to reach a plateau during adulthood.
source: We speculate that, similar to other spindle features, the trajectory of SO-coupling strength is likely to reach a plateau during adulthood (Nicolas et al., 2001; Purcell et al., 2017).
evidence: Speculation based on citations to spindle development literature

claim: Interindividual oscillatory variability was pronounced even in the adult age group.
source: Remarkably, interindividual oscillatory variability was pronounced even in the adult age group (Figure 3A), highlighting the critical need to employ individualized cross-frequency coupling analyses to avoid its pitfalls (Aru et al., 2015; Muehlroth and Werkle-Bergner, 2020).
evidence: Supported by single subject data shown in Figure 3A

claim: There is a critical need to employ individualized cross-frequency coupling analyses to avoid methodological pitfalls.
source: Remarkably, interindividual oscillatory variability was pronounced even in the adult age group (Figure 3A), highlighting the critical need to employ individualized cross-frequency coupling analyses to avoid its pitfalls (Aru et al., 2015; Muehlroth and Werkle-Bergner, 2020).
evidence: Inference from observed variability with citations to methodological literature

claim: Sleep has been shown to support fine-motor memory consolidation in individuals after stroke.
source: As sleep has been shown to support fine-motor memory consolidation in individuals after stroke (Gudberg and Johansen-Berg, 2015; Siengsukon and Boyd, 2008), SO–spindle coupling integrity could be a valuable, easy to assess predictive index for rehabilitation success.
evidence: Supported by citations to stroke rehabilitation studies

claim: SO–spindle coupling integrity could be a valuable, easy to assess predictive index for rehabilitation success.
source: As sleep has been shown to support fine-motor memory consolidation in individuals after stroke (Gudberg and Johansen-Berg, 2015; Siengsukon and Boyd, 2008), SO–spindle coupling integrity could be a valuable, easy to assess predictive index for rehabilitation success.
evidence: Speculation based on current findings and cited stroke studies

claim: Motor learning is a process relying on complex spatial and temporal scales in the human brain.
source: Motor learning is a process relying on complex spatial and temporal scales in the human brain.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about motor learning

claim: To acquire motor skills the brain integrates information from extracortical structures with cortical structures via cortico-striato-thalamo-cortico loops and cortico-cerebello-thalamo-cortico circuits.
source: To acquire motor skills the brain integrates information from extracortical structures with cortical structures via cortico-striato-thalamo-cortico loops and cortico-cerebello-thalamo-cortico circuits (Dayan and Cohen, 2011; Doyon and Benali, 2005; Doyon et al., 2018; Pinsard et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to motor learning literature

claim: Growing evidence advocates for hippocampal recruitment for motor learning, especially in the context of sleep-dependent memory consolidation.
source: However, growing evidence also advocates for hippocampal recruitment for motor learning, especially in the context of sleep-dependent memory consolidation (Albouy et al., 2013; Boyke et al., 2008; Draganski et al., 2004; Pinsard et al., 2019; Sawangjit et al., 2018; Schapiro et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Hippocampal memory reactivation during sleep is one cornerstone of the active systems consolidation theory.
source: Hippocampal memory reactivation during sleep is one cornerstone of the active systems consolidation theory, where coordinated SO–spindle activity route subcortical information to the cortex for long-term storage (Diekelmann and Born, 2010; Helfrich et al., 2019; Klinzing et al., 2019; Ngo et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical framework

claim: Coordinated SO–spindle activity routes subcortical information to the cortex for long-term storage.
source: Hippocampal memory reactivation during sleep is one cornerstone of the active systems consolidation theory, where coordinated SO–spindle activity route subcortical information to the cortex for long-term storage (Diekelmann and Born, 2010; Helfrich et al., 2019; Klinzing et al., 2019; Ngo et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical framework

claim: Higher SO–spindle coupling strength supporting gross-motor learning points toward a more efficient information exchange between hippocampus and cortical areas.
source: Thus, higher SO–spindle coupling strength supporting gross-motor learning in our study points toward a more efficient information exchange between hippocampus and cortical areas.
evidence: Inference from current findings and cited literature on coupling and hippocampal communication

claim: Untrained motor sequences exhibit hippocampal activation that subsides for more consolidated sequences.
source: Recently, it has been found that untrained motor sequences exhibit hippocampal activation that subsides for more consolidated sequences. This change was further accompanied by increased motor cortex activation, suggesting a transformative function of sleep for motor memory (Pinsard et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to recent study

claim: Hippocampal disengagement likely indexes the transition from the fast learning stage to the slower learning stage with more proficient motor skill.
source: In other words, hippocampal disengagement likely indexes the transition from the fast learning stage to the slower learning stage with more proficient motor skill (Dayan and Cohen, 2011; Doyon and Benali, 2005).
evidence: Inference based on citations to motor learning theory

claim: SO-coupling strength represents the extent of hippocampal support for integrating information to motor cortices during complex motor skill learning.
source: Given that our subjects did not reach asymptotic performance level (Figure 2A, B) and that SO–spindle coupling tracks gross-motor skill learning dynamics as it relates to both, learning curve attenuation and task proficiency increments, it is plausible that SO-coupling strength represents the extent of hippocampal support for integrating information to motor cortices during complex motor skill learning.
evidence: Speculation based on current findings and theoretical framework

claim: Striatal network reactivation during sleep was found to be synchronized to sleep spindles, which predicted motor memory consolidation.
source: For example, striatal network reactivation during sleep was found to be synchronized to sleep spindles, which predicted motor memory consolidation (Fogel et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: In primates, coherence between M1 and cerebellum in the SO and spindle frequency range suggested that coupled oscillatory activity conveys information through cortico-thalamo-cerebellar networks.
source: In primates, coherence between M1 and cerebellum in the SO and spindle frequency range suggested that coupled oscillatory activity conveys information through cortico-thalamo-cerebellar networks (Xu et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to primate study

claim: SO–spindle coupling may represent a more general gateway for the brain to exchange subcortical and cortical information and not just hippocampal–neocortical communication.
source: One testable hypothesis for future research is whether SO–spindle coupling represents a more general gateway for the brain to exchange subcortical and cortical information and not just hippocampal–neocortical communication.
evidence: Speculation about broader role of coupling based on cited evidence

claim: The consistency of the SO–spindle interplay identified at electrodes overlapping with motor areas was predictive for the gross-motor learning process.
source: Critically, we found that the consistency of the SO–spindle interplay identified at electrodes overlapping with motor areas such as M1 was predictive for the gross-motor learning process (Figure 3D, E).
evidence: Supported by correlational analyses shown in Figures 3D and 3E

claim: SO–spindle coupling supports the information flow between task-relevant subcortical and cortical areas.
source: This finding corroborates the idea that SO–spindle coupling supports the information flow between task-relevant subcortical and cortical areas.
evidence: Inference from regional specificity of coupling effects

claim: Neural firing patterns in M1 during spindles became more coherent after performing a grasping motor task in rodents.
source: Recent evidence in the rodent model demonstrated that neural firing patterns in M1 during spindles became more coherent after performing a grasping motor task. The extent of neural firing precision was further mediated by a function of temporal proximity of spindles to SOs (Silversmith et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to rodent study

claim: The extent of neural firing precision in M1 was mediated by temporal proximity of spindles to SOs.
source: Recent evidence in the rodent model demonstrated that neural firing patterns in M1 during spindles became more coherent after performing a grasping motor task. The extent of neural firing precision was further mediated by a function of temporal proximity of spindles to SOs (Silversmith et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to rodent study

claim: Coupled spindles are likely to induce neural plasticity that benefits motor learning through synchronizing processes and Ca2+ influx propagating property.
source: Through this synchronizing process and their Ca2+ influx propagating property, coupled spindles are likely to induce neural plasticity that benefits motor learning (Niethard et al., 2018).
evidence: Inference based on citation to mechanistic study

claim: Sleep impacts the learning curve but did not affect task proficiency in comparison to a wake retention interval directly after learning.
source: We found that sleep impacts the learning curve but did not affect task proficiency in comparison to a wake retention interval directly after learning (Figure 2D, E).
evidence: Supported by statistical analyses shown in Figures 2D and 2E

claim: Sleep rather stabilizes than improves gross-motor memory.
source: (1) Sleep rather stabilizes than improves gross-motor memory, which is in line with previous gross-motor adaption studies (Bothe et al., 2019; Bothe et al., 2020).
evidence: Speculation supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Presleep performance is critical for sleep to improve motor skills.
source: (2) Presleep performance is critical for sleep to improve motor skills (Wilhelm et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: Sleep effects are intermingled with time of day effects on juggling performance.
source: (3) Sleep effects are intermingled with time of day effects on juggling performance.
evidence: Inference from the study's findings on time of day effects

claim: The steeper learning curve after the first retention interval in the sleep-first group can also be interpreted as a time of day effect.
source: Indeed, the steeper learning curve after the first retention interval in the sleep-first group can also be interpreted as a time of day effect.
evidence: Inference from the pattern of results

claim: Cognitive performance and motor learning are influenced by the time of day.
source: Additionally, we did not find evidence for a circadian modulation of cognitive engagement based on objective reaction time data in our study (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C). However, a null-result does not exclude all possible circadian effects and ample evidence suggests that cognitive performance and motor learning are influenced by the time of day (Blatter and Cajochen, 2007; Keisler et al., 2007; Tandoc et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to circadian rhythm literature

claim: The study cannot fully disentangle circadian and sleep effects.
source: Therefore, we cannot fully disentangle circadian and sleep effects with our study design, which should be considered a limitation to our findings.
evidence: Acknowledged limitation based on study design

claim: A learning-induced change in coupling strength did not relate to behavior.
source: Moreover, we found that SO–spindle coupling strength remains remarkably stable between two nights, which also explains why a learning-induced change in coupling strength did not relate to behavior (Figure 3—figure supplement 2I).
evidence: Supported by analysis shown in supplementary figure

claim: State and trait effects are not mutually exclusive in spindle literature.
source: Note that state and traits effects are not mutually exclusive. The overlap of state and trait effects is a long-standing issue in spindle literature, which also seems so apply to their coordinated interplay with SOs (Lustenberger et al., 2015; Schabus et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to spindle literature

claim: Subcortical–cortical network communication is likely to be refined throughout brain development.
source: This subcortical–cortical network communication is likely to be refined throughout brain development, since we discovered elevated coupling strength in adults compared to early adolescents (Figure 3C).
evidence: Inference from developmental comparison shown in Figure 3C

claim: SO–spindle coupling precision is enhanced from childhood to late adolescence.
source: This result compliments our earlier findings of enhanced coupling precision from childhood to adolescence (Hahn et al., 2020) and the recently demonstrated lower coupling strength in preschool children (Joechner et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous developmental studies

claim: Preschool children have lower coupling strength than older children.
source: This result compliments our earlier findings of enhanced coupling precision from childhood to adolescence (Hahn et al., 2020) and the recently demonstrated lower coupling strength in preschool children (Joechner et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to recent study

claim: Age severely influences fractal dynamics in the brain.
source: Age severely influences fractal dynamics in the brain (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) and the defining features of sleep oscillations (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in supplementary figures

claim: Age severely influences the defining features of sleep oscillations.
source: Age severely influences fractal dynamics in the brain (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) and the defining features of sleep oscillations (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in figures

claim: Coupled spindles precisely capture corticohippocampal network communication as well as hippocampal ripple expression.
source: Nonetheless, as demonstrated recently, coupled spindles precisely capture corticohippocampal network communication as well as hippocampal ripple expression (Helfrich et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to recent study

claim: Hippocampal engagement is especially crucial at the earlier learning stages.
source: Remarkably, hippocampal engagement is especially crucial at the earlier learning stages.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about motor learning stages

claim: Motor skill learning involves fast and slow learning stages.
source: We hypothesized, that a stronger increase in task proficiency across sleep would lead to a flatter learning curve based on the assumption that motor skill learning involves fast and slow learning stages.
evidence: Based on established motor learning theory

claim: The learning process of complex motor skills consists of a fast initial learning stage during skill acquisition and a much slower skill retaining learning stage.
source: The learning process of complex motor skills is thought to consist of a fast initial learning stage during skill acquisition and a much slower skill retaining learning stage (Dayan and Cohen, 2011; Doyon and Benali, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to motor learning theory

claim: Within-learning session performance gains are rapid at the beginning, but taper off with increased motor skill proficiency, resembling a power-law curve.
source: In other words, within-learning session performance gains are rapid at the beginning, but taper off with increased motor skill proficiency, resembling a power-law curve.
evidence: Based on established motor learning theory

claim: Event co-occurrence is higher in NREM3 than in NREM2.
source: Event co-occurrence is higher in NREM3 (F(1, 51) = 1209.09, p < 0.001, partial eta² = 0.96) as well as in adults (F(1, 51) = 11.35, p = 0.001, partial eta² = 0.18).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of co-occurrence rates

claim: Event co-occurrence is higher in adults than in adolescents.
source: Event co-occurrence is higher in NREM3 (F(1, 51) = 1209.09, p < 0.001, partial eta² = 0.96) as well as in adults (F(1, 51) = 11.35, p = 0.001, partial eta² = 0.18).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of co-occurrence rates

claim: SO phase modulates spindle activity in both age groups.
source: Adolescents and adults revealed a shifting temporal pattern in spindle activity (11–16 Hz) depending on the SO phase. In more detail, spindle activity decreased during the negative peak of the SO ('down-state') but increased during the positive peak ('up-state'). This temporal pattern and the underlying SO component in spindle event detection (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E) confirm the coordinated nature of the two major sleep oscillations in adolescents and adults.
evidence: Supported by time-frequency analysis shown in supplementary figure

claim: Spindle activity decreased during the negative peak of the SO ('down-state') but increased during the positive peak ('up-state').
source: In more detail, spindle activity decreased during the negative peak of the SO ('down-state') but increased during the positive peak ('up-state').
evidence: Supported by time-frequency analysis

claim: The temporal pattern of spindle activity and the underlying SO component confirm the coordinated nature of the two major sleep oscillations in adolescents and adults.
source: This temporal pattern and the underlying SO component in spindle event detection (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E) confirm the coordinated nature of the two major sleep oscillations in adolescents and adults.
evidence: Inference from observed temporal patterns

claim: The significant differences in amplitude from −1.4 to −0.8 s and 0.4–1.5 s are caused by increased coupling strength in adults.
source: Critically, the significant differences in amplitude from −1.4 to −0.8 s (p = 0.023, d = −0.73) and 0.4–1.5 s (p < 0.001, d = 1.1) are not caused by age-related differences in power or different EEG systems but instead by the increased coupling strength (i.e., higher coupling precision of spindles to SOs) in adults giving rise to a more pronounced SO-wave shape when averaging across spindle peak locked epochs.
evidence: Inference from normalized data analysis

claim: Coupling strength is defined as 1 − circular variance.
source: Based on these adjusted phase values, we derived the coupling strength defined as 1 − circular variance.
evidence: Definition of the metric used

claim: Coupling strength describes the consistency of the SO–spindle coupling.
source: This metric describes the consistency of the SO–spindle coupling (i.e., higher coupling strength indicates more precise coupling) and has previously been shown to accurately track brain development and memory formation (Hahn et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous validation

claim: Higher coupling strength indicates more precise coupling.
source: This metric describes the consistency of the SO–spindle coupling (i.e., higher coupling strength indicates more precise coupling) and has previously been shown to accurately track brain development and memory formation (Hahn et al., 2020).
evidence: Definition of the metric interpretation

claim: Coupling strength has previously been shown to accurately track brain development and memory formation.
source: This metric describes the consistency of the SO–spindle coupling (i.e., higher coupling strength indicates more precise coupling) and has previously been shown to accurately track brain development and memory formation (Hahn et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work

claim: There was no difference in electrophysiological parameters between the adolescents of the wake-first and sleep-first groups.
source: Notably, we found no differences in electrophysiological parameters (i.e., coupling strength, event detection) between the adolescents of the wake-first and sleep-first groups (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B and Supplementary file 1—table 8).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison shown in supplementary materials

claim: The relationship between coupling strength, learning curve and task proficiency is independent of age differences.
source: To rule out age as a confounding factor that could drive the relationship between coupling strength, learning curve and task proficiency in the mixed sample, we used cluster-corrected partial correlations to confirm their independence of age differences (task proficiency: mean rho = 0.40, p = 0.017; learning curve: rhos = −0.47, p = 0.049).
evidence: Supported by partial correlation analysis controlling for age

claim: The relationship between coupling strength and learning outcomes is not influenced by individual differences in alertness.
source: Additionally, given that we found that juggling performance could underlie a circadian modulation we controlled for individual differences in alertness between subjects due to having just slept. We partialed out the mean PVT reaction time before the juggling performance test after sleep from the original analyses and found that our results remained unchanged (task proficiency: mean rho = 0.37, p = 0.025; learning curve: rhos = −0.49, p = 0.040).
evidence: Supported by partial correlation analysis controlling for alertness

claim: The correlations between coupling strength and learning outcomes are not influenced by individual differences in SO and spindle event parameters.
source: Further, we also confirmed that our correlations are not influenced by individual differences in SO and spindle event parameters (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by control analyses shown in supplementary figure

claim: Adolescents in the wake-first group had higher task proficiency at the time point of the sleep retention interval due to additional training.
source: Furthermore, given that we only recorded PSG for the adults in the sleep-first group and that adolescents in the wake-first group showed enhanced task proficiency at the time point of the sleep retention interval due to additional training (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A), we only considered adolescents and adults of the sleep-first group to ensure a similar level of juggling experience (for summary statistics of sleep architecture and SO and spindle events of subjects that entered the correlational analyses; see Supplementary file 1—table 7).
evidence: Supported by comparison shown in supplementary figure

claim: Participants without prior juggling experience trained to juggle for 1 hr.
source: Participants without prior juggling experience trained to juggle for 1 hr.
evidence: Description of experimental procedure

claim: The amount of successful three-ball cascades was measured during performance tests in multiple 3-min blocks.
source: We measured the amount of successful three-ball cascades (i.e., three consecutive catches) during performance tests in multiple 3-min blocks (3 × 3 min for adolescents; 5 × 3 min for adults) before and after the respective retention intervals.
evidence: Description of experimental procedure

claim: Adolescents performed fewer blocks than adults to alleviate exhaustion from the extensive juggling training.
source: Adolescents performed fewer blocks than adults to alleviate exhaustion from the extensive juggling training.
evidence: Explanation of experimental design decision

claim: Three consecutive catches qualify as the criteria for the motor task to be considered juggling.
source: We opted for three-ball cascades as a performance index because we considered three consecutive catches as the criteria for the motor task to qualify as juggling (Boyke et al., 2008; Draganski et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to juggling studies

claim: The estimated task proficiency was comparable to the observed values in the corresponding first juggling block.
source: Importantly, the estimated task proficiency was comparable to the observed values in the corresponding first juggling block (performance test 1: rhos = 0.98, p < 0.001; performance test 2: rhos = 0.97, p < 0.001).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis validating the metric

claim: Power differences in the signal can systematically impact cross-frequency coupling measures by changing the signal-to-noise ratio.
source: Power differences in the signal can systematically impact cross-frequency coupling measures by changing the signal-to-noise ratio, which in turn influences the precision of the phase estimation of the signal (Aru et al., 2015; Scheffer-Teixeira and Tort, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to methodological literature

claim: Power decreases are apparent across the lifespan.
source: Because power decreases are apparent across the lifespan (Campbell and Feinberg, 2009; Campbell and Feinberg, 2016; Hahn et al., 2020; Helfrich et al., 2018), we z-normalized all detected SO and spindle events in the time domain to alleviate this possible confound before calculating phase-amplitude coupling measures (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by citations to developmental EEG literature

claim: Cross-frequency coupling renders meaningful information of network communication only when the suspected interacting oscillations are present in the signal.
source: Cross-frequency coupling renders meaningful information of network communication only when the suspected interacting oscillations are present in the signal.
evidence: Based on methodological principles of coupling analysis

claim: Low co-occurrence of SO and spindles in NREM2 can cause spurious coupling estimates.
source: Therefore, we only analyzed SO and sleep spindle epochs during which they co-occurred in a 2.5-s time window (±~2 SO cycles around the spindle peak). Furthermore, we restricted all our coupling analyses to sleep stage NREM3 because of general lower co-occurrence of SO and spindles in NREM2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, D), which can cause spurious coupling estimates (Hahn et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous methodological work
